characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester; load 9.8 N for 15 s
characterization_methods.key_findings: The 17Al alloy aged at 625 °C for 3 h has a Vickers hardness of 872.0 ± 24.4 HV (Table 3); whole alloy series spans 259.8–924.9 HV.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Each sample repeatedly tested 5 times; average of 5 measurements
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the hardness evolution of the 17Al alloy after aging treatments

characterization_methods.key_findings: Both α-Mn and β-Mn diffraction peaks were found, indicating α-Mn and β-Mn coprecipitated during aging before the α matrix fully transformed to β-Mn (the 17Al trace analyzed was aged at 575 °C/1 h, not 625 °C/3 h).
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify phase compositions of the alloys after aging

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV
characterization_methods.key_findings: Increase in Al content slowed the β-Mn precipitation kinetics; for the 17Al alloy the α matrix nearly fully transformed to β-Mn after 6 h at 550 °C and after 1 h at 600 °C and above.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Electrolytically polished samples (10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol)
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify precipitation of secondary phases (α-Mn, β-Mn) in aged samples
characterization_methods.technique: Secondary electron (SE) SEM imaging and EDS analysis

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: GeminiSEM 300 SEM; scanning step size 1.5 μm (low magnification) and 0.05 μm (high magnification)
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 17Al alloy the α matrix progressively transformed to β-Mn and new BCC and FCC precipitates appeared within the β-Mn at higher temperatures (conditions shown: 525 °C/10 h, 575 °C/6 h, 650 °C/10 h).
characterization_methods.purpose: Characterize the α → β-Mn transformation and new BCC/FCC precipitates

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: FEI Talos F200X microscope equipped with an EDS detector, operated at 200 kV
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 17Al alloy (aged 575 °C/6 h) fine FCC Cu-rich particles containing FCC twins precipitate at the β-Mn interfaces; HRTEM/FFT confirmed β-Mn and the FCC Cu-rich phase.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Ion-thinned foils (~90 μm ground, 3 mm punched)
characterization_methods.purpose: Elucidate the fine precipitate structures in the ultra-high hardness alloys
characterization_methods.technique: Transmission electron microscopy (BF/DF imaging, SAED, HRTEM, FFT) with EDS

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Agilent G200 Nanoindenter; indentation depth 200 nm; test points spaced ≥5 μm apart
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the hardest 17Al sample, average nanoindentation hardness = 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa and β-Mn intrinsic hardness = 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa (this is the peak-hardness 17Al sample, 575 °C/6 h).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Mechanically polished samples (to prevent Cu-rich phase flaking)
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure intrinsic micro-hardness of β-Mn and the ultra-hard alloys

characterization_methods.key_findings: Densities of 15Al, 17Al and 19Al alloys are 6.85, 6.76 and 6.66 g·cm⁻³ respectively.

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: FCC twin structure was observed within the Cu-rich particles; the SAED pattern of the Cu-rich region in the 17Al alloy was labelled 'FCC twin' with two superimposed twin-related patterns.

interfaces.interface_notes: For the 17Al alloy, fine FCC Cu-rich particles are distributed at the interfaces of the β-Mn, and the new BCC phase also forms at the interfaces between β-Mn. The FCC Cu-rich phase decreases between β-Mn interfaces with increasing Al content. (These interface features are reported for 17Al aged samples, e.g. 575 °C/6 h TEM in Fig. 12; the 625 °C/3 h condition itself was not separately imaged.)
interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Alloy ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-xAl-5Cu (at.%, x = 15, 17, 19) were produced by melting raw materials of high purity (>99.9 %) using a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere.
Ingots homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h prior to hot rolling.
Homogenized ingots were hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
processing_steps.reduction_ratio: rolled into plates of 4 mm thickness

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Plates were cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples by electrical discharge machining for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Samples solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching. This is the parent process (proc_st-1100c-10min-oq) of the sample.

This is the defining step of the sample: solution-treated 17Al alloy aged at 625 °C for 3 h followed by water quenching. (General schedule: aged at 525–650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h, followed by water quenching.)

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers hardness measured with a load of 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample repeatedly tested 5 times and the average reported.

phases_present.morphology: near-equiaxed matrix grains (α matrix almost completely transformed to β-Mn)
fine particles distributed within the β-Mn
fine particles distributed at the β-Mn interfaces

structures.overall_structure: For the 17Al alloy, at aging temperatures of 600 °C and above the α (BCC) matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn after just 1 h of aging. Thus after aging at 625 °C for 3 h the alloy is essentially a β-Mn matrix containing numerous fine new precipitates (a new BCC phase and an FCC Cu-rich phase) distributed within the β-Mn and at the β-Mn interfaces.

unmapped_findings: 17Al alloy EDS-measured chemical composition (Table 1): Fe 43.2, Mn 34.8, Al 17.0, Cu 5.0 (at.%).
Density of the 17Al alloy measured by Archimedes method = 6.76 g/cm³.
Solution-treated (as-quenched, before aging) Vickers hardness of the 17Al alloy = 259.8 ± 1.5 HV (baseline of the process chain; Table 3).
Full 625 °C aging series for the 17Al alloy (Table 3): 1 h = 813.0 ± 20.8 HV, 3 h = 872.0 ± 24.4 HV (= this sample), 6 h = 878.4 ± 28.3 HV, 10 h = 870.5 ± 24.9 HV.

The peak hardness of the 17Al alloy was 924.9 ± 25.8 HV after aging at 575 °C for 6 h (not at 625 °C); the fracture toughness K_IC of that peak-hardness 17Al sample was 6.6 MPa·m^1/2, and the elastic modulus used for the calculation was 175 GPa.
For the hardest 17Al sample (575 °C/6 h), β-Mn intrinsic hardness = 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa, and SEM-EDS composition of β-Mn = Mn 36.2 at.%, Al 16.3 at.%, Cu 2.6 at.%.
The paper reports the maximum specific hardness of the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu family as 141 HV·cm³/g, achieved by the Fe-35.2Mn-15.0Al-5.2Cu (15Al) alloy — not by the 17Al sample.

No dedicated micrograph/EBSD/TEM/XRD characterization was reported specifically for the 17Al alloy at 625 °C/3 h; the 625 °C aging data for 17Al are limited to the Vickers hardness value/tabulated series and the corresponding contour plot (Fig. 2b). Microstructure descriptions used here reflect the general 17Al aging behavior at ≥600 °C.
The optimal aging temperature range for achieving ultra-high hardness in the 17Al alloy was reported as 550–600 °C (625 °C lies slightly above this window).
